title: ‘Speed, ecstasy, and marijuana. Ice is not on that list’: Pickering details drug use
full_text:
Welcome to The Australian’s rolling coverage of news from Canberra and around the country.
One Nation Treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce has lashed out over the impacts of his party’s plan to unlock compulsory super contributions for seven million renters and mortgage holders around the country.
In an appeal to cash-strapped households, One Nation would allow workers early access to a quarter of their compulsory contributions for up to three years, providing a tax-advantaged bump to Australians’ take-home pay.
During a fiery interview on the ABC’s 7.30 program, Mr Joyce was unable to provide details on how much the average Australian stood to forfeit from the retirement savings should they access the scheme.
It was Mr Joyce’s first 7.30 appearance since his ‘sit down’ snap at his off-screen dog in July.
Pushed by Sarah Ferguson to provide modelling on the loss to people’s savings over time, Mr Joyce claimed he should have been provided with examples before the interview.
“Well, here we go folks. I’ll try and answer something which we could need an annuity table, and we’ll also need sort of lineal regression. I’ll do it for you. Straight down the barrel,” he complained.
“You’ve just come up with a question you haven’t given me the details about it.”
Put to him that he was the party’s treasury spokesman and should have been across the detail, Mr Joyce retorted, “The treasury spokesman, Not Jesus Christ. I mean, you have to actually give me the details of these things if you got to put them forward to me”.
“Well, folks, how on earth. I mean, this is ridiculous. This is like saying, ‘Well, look, I’m now going to give you an incredibly complex question’. Now, Sarah, I’m happy to come back to you tomorrow. And as I said on another stable, and as long as you’re prepared to pay my accountancy fees, we can do this regression analysis,” he said.
It comes amid fervent warnings from economists and the superannuation sector that the policy would further fuel inflation and worsen the cost-of-living pressures it is attempting to remedy.
